content:
The test image shows a single corn plant that has completely wilted/died (all leaves tan/brown and dried) while surrounding plants remain healthy green. This suggests a systemic wilt or stalk rot disease. Key observations:
- Entire plant affected uniformly brown/dead
- Stalk appears to be standing (not collapsed)
- Surrounded by healthy neighbors
- Leaves are dried and hanging

Candidates: Stewarts_wilt, Goss_wilt, Anthracnose stalk rot, Bacterial stalk rot. Let me compare reference images.
The Bacterial stalk rot reference (top-right) shows a plant with completely dead/brown leaves surrounded by healthy green plants — very close to the test image. Let me check more candidates.
The Corn Stunt reference also shows completely dead/dried plants at late stage. Let me check a few more candidates to reach my minimum viewing budget.

I've now viewed 12+ reference images. Let me consolidate my analysis.

**Test image observations:**
- Single corn plant completely dead — all leaves uniformly tan/brown, dried and hanging
- Stalk still standing upright (not collapsed)
- Surrounding plants healthy and green
- Tassel also dead/brown at top
- No visible spots, pustules, mold, freckles, or lesion patterns on leaves

**Candidate elimination:**
- **Gray leaf spot, NCLB, Eyespot** — These show discrete lesions on green leaves, not whole-plant death
- **Charcoal/Diplodia stalk rot** — Reference shows lodged/collapsed plants and internal stalk tissue damage
- **Fusarium** — Ear rot disease, doesn't match
- **Stewarts wilt** — Reference shows young seedling stunting, not mature plant death
- **Goss wilt** — Shows freckles/bacterial exudate on leaves; multiple plants affected; doesn't match single-plant uniform death
- **Physoderma stalk rot** — Plants snap at node; reference field view showed dried plants but those had broken stalks
- **Corn Stunt Spiroplasma** — Shows reddish-purple discoloration and stunting

**Best match: Bacterial stalk rot**
- Reference images (especially bottom-right) showed single plants completely dead with tan/brown uniformly dried leaves, stalk standing, surrounded by healthy green plants — nearly identical to test image
- Bacterial stalk rot causes rapid, complete plant death from vascular/stalk tissue collapse
- The uniform whole-plant death (not piecemeal leaf lesions) strongly suggests a vascular/systemic or stalk issue causing acute death
